title: Apraclonidine: The Alpha-2 Powerhouse
summary: Apraclonidine (Iopidine) is a potent selective alpha-2 adrenergic agonist primarily used for acute intraocular pressure (IOP) control, post-laser prophylaxis, and neuro-ophthalmic diagnosis. While highly effective for short-term use, its clinical utility is limited by rapid tachyphylaxis and high rates of follicular conjunctivitis.

sections.title: Clinical Definition & Classification
sections.content: Apraclonidine is a synthetic sympathomimetic amine, a derivative of clonidine. It acts as a relatively selective alpha-2 adrenergic agonist (though less selective than Brimonidine). It is classified as an ocular hypotensive agent that reduces IOP by decreasing aqueous humor production via the inhibition of adenylate cyclase in the ciliary body.

rows: 1 drop 1 hour pre-op; 1 drop immediately post-op
1 drop TID for up to 4 weeks

sections.title: The 'Reversal' Test: Horner's Syndrome
content: Step 1: Document baseline anisocoria in dim and bright light.
Step 2: Instill one drop of 0.5% or 1.0% Apraclonidine in both eyes.
Step 3: Wait 30 to 45 minutes (up to 60 mins).
Step 4: Pathophysiology: Denervation hypersensitivity causes Mueller's muscle (alpha-1 sensitive) to contract in the Horner's eye.
Step 5: Positive Result: Mydriasis and ptosis resolution (reversal) in the Horner's eye; no effect on the normal pupil.
Step 6: Interpretation: Confirms Horner's but does not localize the lesion (pre- vs. post-ganglionic).

sections.title: Prophylaxis of Post-Laser IOP Spikes
content: Nd:YAG Laser Capsulotomy (reduces risk of transient spikes >10mmHg)
Argon/Selective Laser Trabeculoplasty (ALT/SLT)
Peripheral Iridotomy (LPI)
Laser Iridoplasty
Effectiveness: Reduces the incidence of post-laser spikes from 25-40% down to <2%.

sections.title: Contraindications & Absolute Restrictions
content: Concurrent use of Monoamine Oxidase Inhibitors (MAOIs)
Hypersensitivity to Apraclonidine or Clonidine
Infants and children under age 6 (risk of severe CNS depression)
Severe Coronary Insufficiency or Recent MI
Nursing Mothers (systemic absorption risk)

rows: Loss of IOP lowering efficacy over 1-4 weeks

content.explanation: A: Acute use only (Post-laser); P: Ptosis reversal (Horner's); R: Redness goes away (Blanching); A: Allergy (Follicular reaction).

sections.title: Pediatric Warning: DO NOT USE
content: Risk of life-threatening CNS depression
Severe somnolence and bradycardia in neonates
Hypotension and respiratory distress reported in toddlers
Use alternative IOP lowering agents in pediatric populations

sections.title: Surgical & Perioperative Uses
content: Trabeculectomy: Used post-operatively for early IOP spikes.
Bleb Needling: Pre-treatment to prevent subconjunctival hemorrhage.
Pars Plana Vitrectomy: Acute post-operative pressure management.
Eyelid Surgery: Off-label use to assess Mueller muscle function pre-blepharoplasty.

sections.title: Key Clinical Pearls
content: Always check for MAOI use before prescribing.
Warn patients about the 'washout' effect; it is not for chronic glaucoma management.
In Horner's testing, a negative result in the first week after injury may be a false negative due to lack of receptor upregulation.
Lid retraction can be used to differentiate Horner's from simple anisocoria.

sections.title: Landmark Research Context
sections.content: Early studies by Pollack et al. and Robin et al. (late 1980s) established Apraclonidine 1.0% as the gold standard for preventing the 30mmHg+ IOP spikes often seen after Argon Laser Trabeculoplasty. Its role evolved with the introduction of Brimonidine, which offered better selectivity and safety for chronic use, relegating Apraclonidine to its current 'acute and diagnostic' niche.
